Found via extensive multi-tenant load testing on a real A100-40GB: the formula-based estimate was ~14x higher than real GPU memory for a realistic shape (21.85GB accounted vs 1.56GB actually resident), needlessly throttling effective multi-tenant cache capacity to a fraction of what the hardware supports.
  • The pre-fit admission-control gate (which must stay conservative, since nothing has run yet to measure) is unchanged -- this fix only affects how much of the cache's capacity budget a successfully fitted context is charged.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Found and fixed during an extensive multi-tenant test suite (concurrent users, cache eviction under pressure, leak detection) run against a real GKE A100-40GB deployment, in direct response to a requirement that this service support several concurrent users at scale.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • /readyz now reports real GPU memory (torch.cuda.memory_allocated/memory_reserved) alongside the cache's own byte-accounting, so the two can be compared to catch the estimator drifting from reality or evicted contexts not actually releasing GPU memory.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Added while running an extensive multi-tenant test suite (concurrent users, cache eviction under pressure, regression task, dataset_id reuse, repeated fit/evict cycles) against a real GKE A100-40GB deployment, per the requirement that this service support several users at scale and be tested accordingly.

Initial release. Multi-tenant context caching engine for tabular ICL models (TabICL backend), calibrated memory estimator, estimator-driven test-row chunking, and a Ray Serve deployment. See README.md for full v1 scope and known gaps.

docs.title: Tabular models as tools for coding agents
docs.text:
Coding agents read files and write code well, but they can't learn from a table on their own. tabctx-mcp gives them TabPFN and TabICL as tools, so an agent can answer "which customers will leave, and why?" from a CSV. One MCP server works with Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI. The same tools also run as a JSON command line, and as a pi extension for agents without MCP.

TABCTX_BASE_URL is any tabctx deployment: one you run yourself (see the Quickstart), or Vector's gateway with a vp_ key, as below.

pip install "tabctx[mcp]"
export TABCTX_BASE_URL=https://proxy.vectorinstitute.ai TABCTX_API_KEY=vp_...
claude mcp add tabctx -- tabctx-mcp          # Claude Code (passes its environment on)
codex mcp add tabctx -- tabctx-mcp           # Codex; then in ~/.codex/config.toml, under
                                             #   [mcp_servers.tabctx]:
                                             #   env_vars = ["TABCTX_BASE_URL", "TABCTX_API_KEY"]
gemini mcp add tabctx tabctx-mcp \
  -e 'TABCTX_BASE_URL=$TABCTX_BASE_URL' -e 'TABCTX_API_KEY=$TABCTX_API_KEY'   # Gemini CLI
tabctx-mcp pi-extension > ~/.pi/agent/extensions/tabctx.ts                     # pi (no MCP)

The single quotes matter. Gemini CLI expands $VARS when it starts the server, so the key isn't written into its settings file. Agents without MCP or an extension can run the same tools as shell commands that print JSON: tabctx-mcp fit history.csv --target Churn, tabctx-mcp predict churn current.csv, and so on (tabctx-mcp --help).

Tool What it does inspect_table Columns, their kinds, missing values and likely ids. With a target, the task and class balance. evaluate Held-out accuracy of each model next to a gradient-boosting baseline. fit_model Fits on every labelled row in seconds and saves the model under a name. predict Writes the table with prediction and probability columns, and returns the top-ranked rows. what_if Predicts hand-made rows, or one real row with some columns changed. explain Permutation importance: which columns the model relies on. list_models The models fitted so far, with their targets and features. delete_model Deletes a model: its context on the server and its saved files, which include its training table.

Fitted models live in .tabctx-mcp/ (or $TABCTX_MCP_HOME), so a model fitted in one call is still there for the next. tabctx-mcp skill prints the guide for agents. The readmission demo in examples/agent_demo/ runs the same task with each agent and scores their predictions against what the patients actually did.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
Tabular foundation models like TabICL and TabPFN make predictions in an unusual way: there is no per-dataset training loop. You hand the model a labeled training table and the rows you want predictions for, and it produces answers in a single forward pass -- the training table is the prompt ("in-context learning"). That's what makes them exciting: one pretrained model, any table, no training pipeline.

It also creates a serving problem. Encoding the training table is by far the most expensive part of that forward pass, and it's identical every time you predict against the same training set. Both TabICL and TabPFN know this: each can cache its own encoded training table (both call it their "KV cache") so repeat predictions skip the re-encode. But that cache lives inside one Python estimator object in one process. The moment you want to serve these models -- many users, many datasets, one GPU -- you need things a single object can't give you:

  • keep many datasets' encoded tables cached at once, each addressable by id, isolated per tenant;
  • know how much GPU memory each one costs, evict the coldest when the budget fills, and refuse a request that would OOM the GPU before it runs;
  • route repeat requests to wherever their cached table lives when the service scales past one replica.

tabctx is that layer. The unit it manages is a training table's encoding: one context per table, cached, measured, evicted and routed like any other shared resource. Hosted APIs such as Prior Labs' cache a fitted table on their own servers; tabctx is the open, self-hosted version, for several models at once, on GPUs you run.

It is plain Python on purpose. The heavy math runs in the models' own GPU kernels, so the orchestration around them (the cache, admission, routing) costs little next to a fit or a predict.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Figure: a request enters through Ray Serve's consistent-hash proxy (affinity on the session header) into a TabctxService replica, which resolves the tenant, reads inline JSON rows or a table file (CSV or Parquet, sent with the request or uploaded first), encodes text columns with the context's schema, and coalesces same-context predicts. With several GPUs, a MultiDeviceEngine places each fit on one GPU and routes predicts to the GPU holding the context, from lock-free snapshots; each GPU's engine runs in its own worker process. A GPU's engine validates input, admits a fit on its estimated memory need, keeps encoded contexts in a byte-budgeted LRU cache, and dispatches to whichever backend fit the context. Evicted contexts optionally spill to local disk and reload on their next use, and one host-memory guard admits large fits against the pod's RAM across all its workers. A single-GPU replica calls its one engine directly (editable source: docs/figures/architecture.svg).

The unit everything revolves around is a context: one training table, encoded once by one model, addressed by dataset_id (scoped per tenant) and reused by every later predict() against it. A context carries its payload (the fitted estimator with its kv cache), the model that fit it, its shape, its schema (column names, and the codes of its text columns, so new rows are encoded the same way), plus a measured byte cost. All models deployed on a device share one cache and one memory budget, so admission control sees the whole device's usage regardless of which model a request picks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• TabctxEngine: fit(X, y) returns a dataset_id, predict(dataset_id, X_test) reuses the cached context, and fit_predict() is there for one-shot callers who don't need caching.
  • ContextCacheManager: a multi-tenant, LRU-evictable cache of encoded training contexts, sized against a real memory budget.
  • AdaptiveMemoryEstimator: admission control that starts from a conservative static formula and gets progressively less conservative as the service accumulates real per-fit() GPU measurements, safely (only ever using a real measurement to bound a smaller-or-equal future request, never to extrapolate upward).
  • Chunked prediction: large test sets are automatically split against the memory budget so one oversized request can't crash the whole replica, the failure mode this library exists partly to prevent (the naive one-shot wrapper it replaces did crash this way; see CHANGELOG). Chunks are sized by a measured predict cost model (memory/predict.py): against a kv context a predict's memory follows its test rows and their width, not the training table, so a 100-row predict against a 10,000 x 500 context is one call. A chunk that still OOMs is halved and retried.
  • TabICL's kv-cache, actually on: tabicl ships with its fit-time context cache disabled, which makes every predict() re-encode the whole training set. tabctx enables it by default (TABCTX_KV_CACHE=kv|repr|off), with predictions verified identical to the uncached path -- and loads the pretrained backbone once per process instead of per fit.
  • int8 context cache (TABCTX_KV_PRECISION=int8, the default): TabICL's ICL key/value cache, most of a context, is stored in int8: about half the memory per context, identical labels and metrics on the evaluation sets, probabilities within 0.009 (native for exact).
  • Compiled attention blocks (TABCTX_COMPILE=1, the default): TabICL's attention blocks run through torch.compile, which fuses the memory-bound layer norms and residual adds around each attention kernel. Fits are 1.7-2.2x faster on the GPU with ~20% lower peak memory, and accuracy is unchanged. The compile happens mostly once per worker at startup (~130 s); a call shape the startup didn't cover (very large tables, for one) compiles on first use, ~10 s once per worker.
  • GPU preprocessing (TABCTX_FAST_PREPROCESSING=1, the default): TabICL's per-column Yeo-Johnson fits, most of a fit's CPU time, run vectorized on the GPU (14x faster on a 40k x 100 table) with lambdas matching scikit-learn's to float32 precision.
  • Same-context coalescing (CoalescingPredictor): concurrent requests against one cached context are packed into a single GPU call within a ~5ms window and split back per caller, amortizing per-call overhead without adding concurrent GPU calls (each GPU still runs at most one predict at a time, beside at most one fit).
  • Several GPUs per replica (MultiDeviceEngine): one engine per GPU, each in its own worker process, behind the single-engine API; see Several GPUs in one replica.
  • Host-memory admission (HostMemoryGuard): large TabICL fits stage tens of GiB in host RAM, so calls of 1 GiB or more reserve their estimated host bytes against one budget shared by the pod's workers (first come, first served), so two huge fits queue instead of getting the pod OOM-killed with every tenant's context.

docs.title: Serving many applications from pre-computed contexts
docs.text:
A natural deployment shape for these models: an admin uploads a cohort table for an application, the model encodes it once, the encoded context (TabICL's kv cache) is saved, and end users of that application only ever call predict against it -- one deployment, many applications, each a loaded context. Here is exactly how far the current library gets you and what is still missing.

Works today:

  • Publish an application = fit_file(<table file>, dataset_id=<app>) under the admin's tenant; the context is encoded once and cached on the GPU. The training table's schema (column names, text categories) is recorded on the context, so test tables are encoded the same way and test files are matched to its columns by name.
  • Select an application = predict(<app>, ...) with the same tenant header. Many applications coexist in one deployment under one memory budget; the models can be mixed (model="tabicl-v2", "tabdpt-1.3", "tabpfn-3.5").
  • Save the kv cache to disk = the spill tier (TABCTX_SPILL_DIR). Contexts evicted under memory pressure are serialized (TabICL's shared backbone excluded) and reload transparently on the next predict, and a restarted replica pointed at the same directory can reload its predecessor's spilled contexts -- no training data needed.

Missing (see ROADMAP.md, item 1):

  1. Explicit, durable persistence. Spilling happens only on eviction, to replica-local disk, best-effort and LRU-bounded. There is no "persist this context" call, no pinning (exempt from eviction), and no shared store (object storage / PVC) a fresh replica or a second deployment could load from. Contexts that were never evicted are lost on restart.
  2. Offline pre-computation. Encoding only happens through the serving endpoint. Publishing an application should also work as a batch job that fits and writes the context to the shared store, with the deployment warm-loading a manifest of contexts at start.
  3. A catalog. GET /v1/tabctx/datasets (0.19) lists a tenant's contexts with their model, task, shape and residency (resident / spilled), and DELETE removes one. Still missing: the schema in the listing, and a persisted state once item 1 exists.
  4. Roles. Tenancy is namespacing, not authorization: a tenant that can predict can also re-fit or evict. "Admin publishes, users predict" needs scoped credentials at the gateway (or read-only tenant tokens).
  5. Per-application endpoints. /v1/apps/<app>/predict is a thin alias onto (tenant, dataset_id, model) and belongs in the gateway or a small application resource, not in the engine.
  6. Portable context format. Serialized contexts are pickled estimators tied to the tabicl/torch versions and device they were fit on. A durable store needs a versioned format with a compatibility check and a fallback to re-fit from the stored table.

docs.title: Deploy on Kubernetes
docs.text:
The Helm chart in deploy/helm/tabctx runs one tabctx server on a GPU node, with a volume that keeps model weights and compiled kernels across restarts.

# From a clone of the repository:
helm install tabctx ./deploy/helm/tabctx

# From a release, once the chart is published with one:
helm install tabctx oci://ghcr.io/vectorinstitute/charts/tabctx --version <version>

Then:

kubectl port-forward svc/tabctx 8000:8000
curl localhost:8000/v1/models

The chart serves TabICLv2 by default. --set 'models={tabicl,tabdpt}' adds TabDPT (both licensed for commercial use; images from 0.19.0), and tabpfn needs a token.

To try it on a cluster without GPUs (kind, minikube), shrink it:

helm install tabctx ./deploy/helm/tabctx --set gpus=0 \
  --set resources.requests.cpu=1 --set resources.requests.memory=4Gi \
  --set resources.limits.memory=4Gi --set weightsCache.sizeGi=5

docs.title: What it creates
docs.text:
• A Deployment of one pod running python -m tabctx.serve, with the GPUs you ask for (gpus), and probes on /livez (startup and liveness) and /readyz (readiness).
  • A Service on port 8000.
  • A PersistentVolumeClaim for weights and compiled kernels (weightsCache), kept when the release is uninstalled; and one for the disk tier if you turn it on (spill).
  • A Secret for TabPFN's token, if you give the token itself.

The pod runs as the image's non-root user with no added capabilities and the runtime's default seccomp profile, so it fits a namespace that enforces the Pod Security "restricted" level.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Value Default Sets models [tabicl] TABCTX_BACKEND Models to serve; the first is the default. gpus 1 nvidia.com/gpu GPUs per pod; 0 runs on the CPU. gpuMemoryFraction 1.0 TABCTX_GPU_MEMORY_FRACTION Share of each GPU tabctx budgets for. requireTenant true TABCTX_REQUIRE_TENANT Every request names its tenant. spill.enabled, spill.sizeGi false, 100 TABCTX_SPILL_DIR The disk tier; tabctx fills at most 90% of it. weightsCache.enabled, .sizeGi, .existingClaim true, 20 HF_HOME, ... Weights and compiled kernels. existingTabpfnSecret / tabpfnToken TABPFN_TOKEN Required with tabpfn. extraEnv, extraVolumes, extraVolumeMounts Any other setting; a name the chart sets is replaced by yours. nodeSelector, tolerations, affinity, resources Placement and size.

values.yaml documents every value.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
• GPU memory bounds how many fitted tables a pod keeps: tabctx admits each fit against its budget for the GPU and evicts the least recently used tables to make room.
  • Host memory: requests equal limits by default, because tabctx budgets large fits against the limit (85% of it, less 8 GiB). Large fits stage data in host memory, by tabctx's own estimates up to about 5 KB per cell for a TabICL table too large for the GPU (5 GB per million cells) and 600 bytes per cell for TabPFN. Size resources.limits.memory for the largest tables you will fit.
  • Scratch: uploads and TabICL's staging go to an emptyDir at /tmp (tmp.sizeLimit, 50 GiB).

docs.title: Exposing it
docs.text:
Put an authenticating gateway in front: tabctx trusts the tenant header as sent, so the gateway must authenticate each caller, set x-tabctx-tenant-id itself and strip any value the client sent. Whatever proxies it needs large bodies and long timeouts: tables up to 4 GiB (TABCTX_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES) and fits that can take minutes. With ingress-nginx, for example:

nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "4g"
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "900"
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "900"

docs.title: Upgrades and restarts
docs.text: A fitted table lives in the server's memory. A restart (an upgrade, a reschedule) drops every table it holds: clients get 404 and fit again, which the scikit-learn estimators do on their own. Tables already evicted to the disk tier, when it is on, come back on their next predict. On shutdown, in-flight requests get terminationGracePeriodSeconds (300) to finish. Each start loads the weights and compiled kernels from the weights volume; the first start downloads and compiles them (startupSeconds, 1200, allows for it; raise it for several models).

docs.title: Several GPUs and replicas
docs.text: Give one pod more GPUs (gpus: 4): tabctx places each table on one of them, with one worker process per GPU. Keep replicaCount: 1: the volumes are ReadWriteOnce, and a fitted table lives in one pod, so several replicas need a router that sends every request for a dataset to the pod that holds it. The chart refuses replicaCount > 1 with its volumes.

docs.title: Offline clusters
docs.text: Pre-fill a volume with the weights (HF_HOME/hub for TabICL and TabDPT, TABPFN_MODEL_CACHE_DIR for TabPFN), give it as weightsCache.existingClaim, and add HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 to extraEnv. With TabPFN's weights already there, tabpfnWithoutToken: true skips the token check.

docs.title: TabPFN
docs.text: TabPFN's weights need a token from Prior Labs after you accept their terms, and are licensed for non-commercial use. Put the token in a Secret with a TABPFN_TOKEN key and name it in existingTabpfnSecret (a token given as tabpfnToken is stored in the release).

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: GET /readyz reports the cache (cache_stats), the GPU memory torch really holds (real_gpu_memory, measured every 5 s; device_report_age_s says how long ago), host memory, and the server's uptime: a burst of 404s with a reset uptime means a restart, not an eviction.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Nearly everything the original roadmap tracked has shipped and been validated on real hardware -- see CHANGELOG.md v0.6.0-v0.9.0 for what landed and the measured evidence. This file now holds only the remainder (each item is also a GitHub issue labelled roadmap), and gets deleted when it empties.

docs.title: Remaining
docs.text:
1. Application catalog + persistent context store (#6) (asked for by the first prospective users, 2026-09-01: "upload a cohort table per application, run TabICLv2 once, save the kv cache to disk, let end users just pick their application"). What exists and what's missing is spelled out in docs/how-it-works.md, "Serving many applications from pre-computed contexts"; the build order that falls out of it:
  2. A ContextStore protocol (persist / load / list / delete by id) with a local-directory implementation first and an object-storage one second; the existing DiskSpillStore becomes the eviction tier on top of it. Contexts gain a pinned flag (never evicted) and a persisted state; serialized files carry tabctx / backend / torch versions and device so a mismatch re-fits instead of loading garbage.
  3. POST /v1/tabctx/datasets/{id}/persist, DELETE /v1/tabctx/datasets/{id} (today nothing but LRU pressure removes a context), GET /v1/tabctx/datasets (per tenant: task, model, shape, feature names, residency), a warm-load manifest at replica start, and a batch tabctx fit entry point that writes to the store without a serving replica.
  4. Read-only tenant credentials at the gateway so "admin publishes, users predict" is enforceable; per-application aliases stay a gateway concern.
  5. Post-release: ephemeral GKE stress run + researcher deployment (#7) (deliberately sequenced after the release). Everything is staged in VectorInstitute/inference-platform branch test/tabicl-gke-onboard: the research overlay (tabctx-research-values.yaml: both models, one A100, spillover, 64Gi host RAM per the measured host-OOM boundary), probes (probe_models.py, probe_stress_v09.py, plus the existing battery), and a parameterized onboard.sh (OVERLAY=... RELEASE=tabctx-research TABPFN_TOKEN=... KEEP_ALIVE=true). The prod inference-platform deployment for Vector researchers follows.
  6. TabPFN memory calibration grid (#8): the preloaded admission grid is TabICL data; TabPFN deployments fall back to the conservative formula plus runtime learning. Run benchmarks/calibrate_memory.py-style sweeps through TabPFNBackend on an A100 and add the grid.
  7. Docs site (#9): README carries the full story today; a docs site matters as external adoption starts.

docs.title: Throughput and table size: multi-GPU and CUDA-level work
docs.text:
Serving gains come first from memory management and scheduling, then from CUDA kernels. tabctx already has the scheduling layer (context cache, usage-aware admission, evict-ahead, spill, same-context coalescing). This track adds multi-GPU replicas and the kernel work. Everything is developed and tested on a GKE GPU node first, then validated on prod's A40s (Ampere sm_86: no FlashAttention-3, no FP8).

  1. Multi-GPU replica (#30, done -- PR #38/#40): one engine per device, fits placed where they fit without eviction on the least active device, predicts routed to the owning device. One worker process per GPU (#39): fits are host-bound (the driving thread is busy ~90% of wall time), so threads of one process contend for the GIL -- 4x A100, four concurrent fits: 2.1-3.1x aggregate from threads, 3.96-4.3x from processes. Under Ray Serve, 6 mixed users: 2.58 -> 5.0 predicts/s.
  2. Profiling (#31, first pass done): a 40k x 100 TabICL fit on an A100 is ~30% CPU preprocessing (per-feature Yeo-Johnson power transforms in scipy dominate) and ~70% GPU half, which is ~87% GPU-busy (flash attention 35%, layer norm 21% -- memory-bound over [4, 40, 40000, 128] activations -- copies 15%). Done from it: the CPU half is prepared before taking the device (overlaps another fit's GPU half: back-to-back fits 17-26% faster), and tabicl's per-call log(n) host-to-device syncs are cached (bit-identical; 10k x 50 fits 16% faster), and the attention blocks are compiled (#36, below). The CPU half's Yeo-Johnson fits are vectorized on the GPU (backends/yeo_johnson.py: 40k x 100 3.38 -> 0.25 s, lambdas within one float32 ulp of scikit-learn's, accuracy unchanged on the evaluation sets). An isolated 40k x 100 fit: 11.2 -> 7.7 s (compiled) -> 4.8 s (both). TabPFN-3.5's fit is the same shape: RMS norm 33% of its CUDA time, flash attention 26%, copies 16%.
  3. Per-device calibration grids (#37, TabPFN done): TabPFN-3.5 has its own requirement grid (A100, 20 shapes): it, too, sizes working memory from what is free, so admission reaches 100k rows at 100 features on an A40 (was 5k on an L4 under TabICL's formula). Still to do: L4/A40- measured grids (A100 grids scale by capacity today; A40 time on GKE doesn't exist, so the A40 grid comes from prod once tabctx runs there). Compiled TabICL has its own A100 grid: its minimum need is up to ~2 GiB above eager's.
  4. Head-of-line scheduling (#39, done): light predicts (resident context, <= 2048 rows) run beside a fit on the same GPU instead of waiting for it -- ~0.1 s p50 during a 40k x 100 fit instead of its full 11 s, 0 wrong answers (thread-local backbone cache); in-use contexts are pinned against evict-ahead; restores and large predicts wait. Small-fit p95 under load 10.6 s -> 1.4 s.
  5. Tiled/fused column+row stage kernels (#32): cut the fit peak and the memory-bound layer norms, raising the per-GPU table ceiling.
  6. Paged context KV + cross-context varlen predict (#33, measured; redirected): batching several tenants' predicts into one GPU call only pays if predicts are GPU-bound, and they aren't. A100, compiled, 32 contexts of 2,000 x 20, 100-row predicts (benchmarks/ bench_predict_throughput.py): ~21 predicts/s per GPU at 1 to 8 concurrent users, latency growing linearly, GPU ~20% busy. A predict is ~47 ms of host-side kernel launches (dynamo dispatch, Triton and cuBLAS launches over ~36 block calls), so the levers are host overhead: CUDA graphs for the predict path (shapes vary: bucket test rows), or two worker processes per GPU for predict-heavy loads. Cross-context KV paging matters again once predicts are launch-free.
  7. INT8 context KV (#34, done for TabICL): ~0.52x resident, identical labels on the evaluation sets; TabPFN already defaults to int8.
  8. Context parallelism across GPUs (#35, not started): tables larger than one GPU (ring attention over the replica's devices). Needs model- level changes in tabicl's attention (its InferenceManager owns batching and offload), so it waits for a workload that exceeds one A40: disk offload already lets one A100 fit 130k x 500 (65M cells) in 26 min, and prod's A40s have 48 GB.
  9. torch.compile (#36, done for TabICL): each attention block's forward compiled, so Inductor fuses the layer norms, residual adds and GELU MLP around the attention kernel. A100: GPU half 1.7-2.2x faster (40k x 100: 7.65 -> 4.30 s), peak memory ~20% lower (33.1 -> 27.0 GiB unconstrained -- but not the minimum a fit needs, which tabicl's free-memory batch sizing sets; compiled needs up to ~2 GiB more at some shapes, so it has its own requirement grid), accuracy unchanged on the evaluation sets; Ray Serve, 6 users on 4x A100: 5.78 -> 6.99 predicts/s. Dynamic shapes needed tabicl's ssmax log(n) computed symbolically (math.log on the row count recompiled every new table). ~50 graphs (fp16 path only) compile in warmup (~130 s per worker); dynamo's settings are applied per call, since its config overrides are per thread and serving calls from other threads (#47). CUDA graphs aren't worth it: the GPU half is GPU-bound, not launch-bound. TabPFN-3.5's own compile path (enable_torch_compile) measured 1.3-1.5x faster fits, ~30% faster predicts and ~22% lower peak, but it still recompiles for many new table sizes (9-82 s each, even with its chunked-SDPA loop kept out of the graph), so it stays off until those are traced down.
  10. Serving-framework-agnostic core (#39): the router, per-GPU workers and scheduling are plain Python with no Ray dependency, so a Dynamo worker can host the same core. Placement is a pluggable policy (placement.py: the router hands it a lock-free view of each device) and the router emits residency events (events.py: placed/removed, to any sink; /v1/tabctx/residency serves the latest), so a platform scheduler can follow where contexts live and steer tabular work around GPUs it wants for LLMs. Next: a Dynamo worker and event-plane sink once the platform moves.

PyTorch-level first: tiling and chunking, torch.compile (generated Triton kernels, CUDA graphs via reduce-overhead), FlexAttention for paged and cross-context attention, SDPA, and torch.distributed context parallelism. Hand-written Triton/CUDA only where a profile (#31) shows a gap those can't close -- the models change too often (TabPFN v3 -> v3.5, TabICL v1 -> v2 within months) for version-locked kernels to be the default.

docs.title: Standing process note
docs.text: Every significant fix in this project came from testing against real systems -- most recently the shared-backbone kv-cache pin (a ~15GB eviction leak) and the fragmentation OOM at 90% budget, both of which only reproduce on a real GPU. Keep reading model internals AND deploying before believing anything.

docs.title: Serving tabctx
docs.text: How to install, run and talk to a tabctx deployment, and how it scales.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Requires Python ≥ 3.12.

pip install tabctx               # core library (FakeBackend, no GPU deps)
pip install "tabctx[tabicl]"     # + real TabICL backend (torch, tabicl)
pip install "tabctx[tabpfn]"     # + TabPFN backend (weights license-gated:
                                 #   ux.priorlabs.ai + export TABPFN_TOKEN)
pip install "tabctx[serve]"      # + Ray Serve deployment (ray[serve], fastapi,
                                 #   pyarrow and python-multipart for table files)
pip install "tabctx[standalone]" # + the Ray-free host (python -m tabctx.serve):
                                 #   [serve] minus ray, single replica only
pip install "tabctx[client]"     # + scikit-learn estimators (scikit-learn, pyarrow, pandas)
pip install "tabctx[dev]"        # + test dependencies

docs.title: Ways to run it
docs.text:
See it work with zero setup (no GPU, no model download: a fake backend stands in for TabICL):

pip install tabctx
curl -sO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/VectorInstitute/tabctx/main/examples/local_fit_predict.py
python local_fit_predict.py

Use it for real, with TabICL doing the actual predicting:

pip install "tabctx[tabicl]"

from tabctx import TabctxEngine, ContextCacheManager
from tabctx.backends.tabicl import TabICLBackend
from tabctx.memory import AdaptiveMemoryEstimator, PowerLawMemoryEstimator, A100_40GB_TABICL_CALIBRATION

estimator = AdaptiveMemoryEstimator(fallback=PowerLawMemoryEstimator(A100_40GB_TABICL_CALIBRATION))
cache = ContextCacheManager(capacity_bytes=estimator.ceiling_bytes())
engine = TabctxEngine(backend=TabICLBackend(), cache=cache, estimator=estimator)

# task is inferred from y_train when omitted (non-integer numbers, or many
# distinct whole numbers such as prices, mean regression); pass
# task="classification" or "regression" to be explicit. Missing values
# (NaN, or null in JSON) are fine: every model handles them.
dataset_id = engine.fit(X_train, y_train)
result = engine.predict(dataset_id, X_test, return_proba=True)

# The whole point: reuse the same cached context for a new test batch,
# with no re-fit cost.
result2 = engine.predict(dataset_id, other_X_test)

Serve it over HTTP with Ray Serve: src/tabctx/serve/app.py is a ready-to-run deployment (fit/predict endpoints, health checks, live memory-usage reporting). See benchmarks/README.md for how to measure it once it's running.

Or without Ray: python -m tabctx.serve (the standalone extra) serves the same endpoints from one plain uvicorn process -- for platforms that don't run Ray, e.g. a Kubernetes Deployment behind a gateway. One replica only (the multi-replica session-affinity router is Ray's); point the platform's liveness probe at GET /livez and its readiness probe at GET /readyz. serve/standalone.py documents what else the Ray host provided and what replaces it.

Talk to a deployment as a scikit-learn model (see the Quickstart), or with the bundled client (pure stdlib, sets the routing/tenancy headers for you, raises the same tabctx exceptions the in-process engine does):

from tabctx import TabctxClient

client = TabctxClient("http://localhost:8000", tenant_id="acme")
client.fit(X_train, y_train, dataset_id="churn-v1")
result = client.predict("churn-v1", X_test, return_proba=True)
client.fit_file("train.parquet", target="churned", dataset_id="churn-v2")

docs.title: Table files and text columns
docs.text:
A fit or predict can send its table as rows of JSON, or as a file in the same request (multipart/form-data, a file part beside the other fields as form fields):

curl $URL/v1/tabctx/fit -F model=tabicl-v2 -F dataset_id=churn -F target=churned -F file=@train.parquet
curl $URL/v1/tabctx/predict -F dataset_id=churn -F file=@test.csv
  • Formats, detected from the content: CSV with a header row (plain, gzip or zstd) and Parquet. Parquet keeps types and nulls and is several times smaller than JSON (a 5,000 x 500 float table: 51 MB as JSON, 13 MB as Parquet), so it is the way to send a large table.
  • Text columns ("gold", "CA") work in files and JSON rows alike: the server codes each text column's values at fit (tabctx.schema), keeps that encoding with the context, and applies it at predict; a value the training table never had becomes missing. Missing values: JSON null, a Parquet null, or a CSV cell that is empty or NA, N/A, null, None, NaN.
  • Columns of a test file are matched to the training file's by name: any order, and extra columns (such as the target) are ignored. A missing one is a 422.
  • The target is target (or target_column), default the last column.

Tables too big for GPU and host memory together can still fit: TabICL offloads stage outputs to memory-mapped files under TABCTX_OFFLOAD_DIR (default <TABCTX_SPILL_DIR>/offload), slower but without exhausting the pod's RAM (one A100 fit 130k x 500 this way).

A file can also be uploaded first and referenced by id, for one that should travel apart from the request that uses it (uploads stream straight to the serving replica's disk):

client = TabctxClient("http://localhost:8000")
upload_id = client.upload_csv_file("train.csv", dataset_id="churn-v1")
client.fit_uploaded(upload_id, "churn-v1", target_column="label")

test_upload = client.upload_csv_file("scoring_batch.csv", "churn-v1")
result = client.predict("churn-v1", test_upload_id=test_upload)
  • Uploads are single-use (consumed by the fit/predict that references them) and expire after TABCTX_UPLOAD_TTL_S (default 1h); size-capped by TABCTX_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (default 4GiB, enforced mid-stream).
  • Uploads are replica-local, so in multi-replica deployments the upload request must carry the same x-session-id: <dataset_id> header as everything else -- affinity routes the upload, fit, and predicts to one replica. (The bundled client does this for you.)
  • Transport size and admission are separate layers: a huge file uploads fine, and the memory-admission gate then decides whether the table fits the GPU budget (413 if not).

docs.title: Scaling out: multi-replica serving
docs.text:
The context cache is in-process and per-replica, so at num_replicas >= 2 requests for one dataset must consistently reach the replica that holds its context. The deployment ships with Ray Serve's consistent-hash request router (requires ray >= 2.58) configured for strict session affinity, and the contract is simply: send the dataset_id as the x-session-id header on every /v1/tabctx/fit and /v1/tabctx/predict call.

curl -X POST $URL/v1/tabctx/fit \
  -H "content-type: application/json" -H "x-session-id: my-dataset" \
  -d '{"train_X": [[1,2],[3,4]], "train_y": [0,1], "dataset_id": "my-dataset"}'

curl -X POST $URL/v1/tabctx/predict \
  -H "content-type: application/json" -H "x-session-id: my-dataset" \
  -d '{"dataset_id": "my-dataset", "test_X": [[5,6]]}'

Details worth knowing:

  • fit() adopts the header value as the dataset_id if the body omits one; a header/body mismatch is rejected 422 (a silent mismatch would mis-route).
  • Omitting the header still works, but only routes correctly on single-replica deployments.
  • Affinity is strict (no fallback replica): if the owning replica is backpressured, callers see retry-with-backoff/503 rather than a spurious 404 from a replica that doesn't hold the context.
  • Responses report served_by (the replica tag) so affinity is observable and testable end to end.
  • When replicas share one physical GPU (e.g. 2 replicas at num_gpus: 0.5), set TABCTX_GPU_MEMORY_FRACTION (e.g. 0.45) so each replica budgets its share of GPU memory. The budget is the visible device's real memory (an L4's 24GB, an A100's 40GB), detected at startup and reported by /readyz as gpu_capacity_bytes.
  • If the deployment renames the affinity header (RAY_SERVE_SESSION_ID_HEADER_KEY), construct the client with session_header= to match; the header name is the routing key.
  • TABCTX_BACKEND=fake runs the whole serve stack without a GPU or torch -- tests/integration/test_multi_replica_affinity.py uses it to prove the multi-replica contract on a laptop.

docs.title: Several GPUs in one replica
docs.text:
A replica that can see several GPUs serves from all of them (TABCTX_DEVICES=auto, the default, or an explicit cuda:0,cuda:1,...): one engine per GPU, with its own backends, cache and spill directory, behind the same API. No client changes and no routing header needed.

  • Placement. Each fit goes to a GPU where the table fits without evicting anyone, preferring the least active GPU (calls in flight, then calls in the last 30s). If no GPU can take it without eviction, it goes to the GPU with the most headroom. Concurrent users spread across GPUs, and a large table gets a whole GPU's headroom.
  • Predicts run on the GPU that holds the context, including after a spill and restore, or a replica restart.
  • Limits. Neither TabICL nor TabPFN can split one context across GPUs, so a table's ceiling is one GPU's memory. What more GPUs buy is N x the resident cache and N fits/predicts in flight at once.
  • Concurrency. Routing reads lock-free snapshots, so it never waits on a GPU's work: fits and predicts on different GPUs run at the same time. Fits and evicts of the same dataset_id are serialized, so a retried fit can't leave two copies. A re-fit lands first and only then replaces the old copy: a failed re-fit (413, OOM) leaves the previous context serving.
  • A process per GPU. Each GPU's engine runs in its own worker process (TABCTX_WORKER_PROCESSES=1, the default with several GPUs; 0 runs them as threads). Fits are host-bound, so threads would contend for Python's GIL: on 4x A100, four concurrent fits ran at ~4x aggregate from processes and 2-3x from threads. A worker that dies fails the replica's health check, so the serving framework restarts it.
  • Small predicts don't wait for fits. A predict of up to 2,048 rows against a resident context runs beside a fit on the same GPU (~0.1 s instead of the fit's full duration); larger predicts and restores of spilled contexts wait their turn.
  • Placement is pluggable. The rule above is the default PlacementPolicy (tabctx.placement); pass your own to MultiDeviceEngine(placement=...) to steer tabular work, e.g. away from a GPU a platform scheduler wants for an LLM. Each placement and removal is a residency event (tabctx.events) for any subscriber; GET /v1/tabctx/residency returns the latest.
  • The replica must be given the GPUs. Under Ray Serve that means ray_actor_options.num_gpus: N, or, for a num_gpus: 0 actor on a GPU pod (as in inference-platform's prod config), RAY_EXPERIMENTAL_NOSET_CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1. A standalone host (python -m tabctx.serve) simply sees the process's CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, nothing extra.
  • Spill. Each GPU spills to its own subdirectory (cuda_0/, ...); TABCTX_SPILL_CAPACITY_BYTES is the replica's total, split evenly. Changing between one and several GPUs changes the layout, and the replica logs a warning about spilled files it won't restore.
  • /readyz reports per-device contexts, bytes, activity and real GPU memory (real_gpu_memory keeps its flat fields, summed, plus per_device); /v1/tabctx/limits reports the best single GPU's headroom and each device's.

docs.title: Listing and deleting contexts
docs.text:
GET /v1/tabctx/datasets lists the contexts the replica holds for the caller's tenant, resident or spilled to disk: id, model, task, shape, size, location, GPU and fit time. It shows metadata only, never a table. DELETE /v1/tabctx/datasets/{dataset_id} removes one from device memory, host memory and the disk tier on every GPU of the replica. It answers 404 if there is none, and 503 if it can't be done right now (retry; the client does).

client = TabctxClient("http://localhost:8000", tenant_id="acme")
client.datasets()            # [{"dataset_id": "churn-v1", "model": "tabicl-v2", ...}]
client.delete("churn-v1")    # DatasetNotFoundError if it isn't there

curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/datasets
curl -X DELETE localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/datasets/churn-v1

What a delete covers:

  • The context and its spilled copy. A predict already running on it finishes, then its memory is freed. A spill or restore of it in progress lands first, so no copy reappears afterwards; if one doesn't land in time the delete answers 503 and deleted nothing.
  • Every GPU, or none. While a GPU worker is down, list and delete answer 503: that worker's spilled copies stay on disk until the replica restarts it, and would come back. If one GPU fails mid-delete, the others are already cleared and the answer is 503; the retry finishes the job.
  • Uploaded tables are already gone: an upload is deleted as soon as the fit or predict that used it has read it, and unused uploads expire after TABCTX_UPLOAD_TTL_S.
  • Retention. A fit can set ttl_s (client.fit(..., ttl_s=3600)), counted from when the fit request arrives, and the server can cap every table with TABCTX_MAX_CONTEXT_AGE_S (tables fit before it was set included). At that time the context is deleted from every tier, with its recorded schema, used or not: a predict after it is a 404, and a sweep every 30 s deletes contexts nobody asks for. Fit responses and the listing show expires_at; the listing leaves out expired tables. The scikit-learn estimators take ttl_s too; they keep their training table and fit again when the server no longer has it, expired or evicted, so a later predict re-uploads the table under a new deadline.
  • One tenant's ids only. Another tenant's context of the same name is untouched. Callers without a tenant id never see scoped contexts, and can't name one: ids starting with t: are reserved for them (422).

With several Ray replicas, a listing comes from whichever replica answers (served_by) and shows only that replica's contexts. The client sends a delete with x-session-id: <dataset_id>, so it reaches the replica that holds the context.

docs.title: Tenant isolation
docs.text:
dataset_id alone is a flat, guessable namespace -- without isolation, any caller who knows another tenant's dataset_id could predict against their cached model. The serving layer therefore scopes every dataset_id by the x-tabctx-tenant-id header before it touches the cache: two tenants can both call their dataset mnist and get fully separate contexts, and a caller without the right tenant id sees a clean 404, never another tenant's model.

  • Set TABCTX_REQUIRE_TENANT=true in production: every /v1/tabctx request must then carry a tenant id (else 401), so there is no unscoped namespace at all.
  • By default the header is optional (dev-friendly, backward compatible), but then unscoped ids coexist with scoped ones and the boundary is advisory, not enforced.
  • Tenant identity is caller-supplied and unverified by design; put an authenticating proxy (API keys -> tenant id) in front for real security. See src/tabctx/serve/tenancy.py for the full trust-model notes.

docs.title: Why a server
docs.text:
TabPFN, TabICL and TabDPT are good models with small, friendly Python packages: fit, then predict, in your own process. That is the right tool for a notebook. This page is about what changes when a model like this becomes something other people and programs depend on, and what tabctx does at each step.

tabctx calls a fitted table a context: the model's encoding of the training table, kept in GPU memory and addressed by an id. In code, the change is one estimator:

from tabctx import TabctxClassifier, TabctxClient

clf = TabctxClassifier(client=TabctxClient("http://my-server:8000"))   # was TabICLClassifier()
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
clf.predict_proba(X_test)

docs.title: Many predictions against one table
docs.text:
A fitted table is reused for every later prediction: a scoring job, an API behind an app, an agent asking what-ifs. Users of these models run large numbers of predictions against one fit (TabPFN #1221).

tabctx: both packages can keep the encoded table inside one estimator object (TabICL's is off by default; tabctx turns it on). tabctx keeps it in a server instead, so every process, job and user predicting against the table shares it and nobody fits it again. Predicts that arrive together for the same table are batched into one GPU call. On an A40, a 100-row predict against a 100,000 × 100 table (TabICLv2) takes about 0.3 s, against 103 s to fit it (benchmarks).

docs.title: Many tables on one GPU
docs.text:
One process with one fitted object holds one table. A service holds many: one per customer, product or experiment. Their encodings are large: a TabICL encoding of 40,000 × 250 is about 5 GB (tabicl #92; TabICL's repr mode, TABCTX_KV_CACHE=repr in tabctx, is much smaller).

tabctx: the tables share a memory budget per GPU. When it is full, the least recently used table is evicted, or written to local disk (TABCTX_SPILL_DIR) and restored on its next predict. GET /v1/tabctx/datasets lists what is held, and DELETE removes it.

docs.title: Running out of GPU memory
docs.text:
Out-of-memory errors come up as table sizes and versions change (TabPFN #849), and users ask to set a device-memory budget instead of the model probing for one by catching out-of-memory errors (tabicl #177).

tabctx: before a fit runs, tabctx estimates its peak GPU memory from the table's shape (using measurements of earlier fits) and checks it against the GPU's budget minus what the tables already held there take. If it fits only after freeing memory, the least recently used tables are evicted first; if it can never fit, it is refused with an error (HTTP 413) before any GPU work, and the server keeps serving everyone else. TABCTX_GPU_MEMORY_FRACTION sets the share of each GPU that budget covers.

docs.title: Keeping a fit
docs.text:
Saving a fitted model in one session and loading it in another has come up for both packages (TabPFN #412, now supported; tabicl #12). On a hosted API, the provider decides how long a fitted table lives (TabPFN #1385).

tabctx: a table stays in the server, under an id you choose, until you delete it or memory pressure evicts it. With a disk tier, an evicted table is written to local disk and comes back on its next predict, also after a server restart on the same node; a table still in GPU memory at a restart is lost. The scikit-learn estimators keep their training table and fit again when the server no longer has it. Durable, shared storage of fitted tables is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Uncertainty
docs.text:
These models predict a distribution, not just a number. TabPFN and TabICL return its quantiles in-process; tabctx returns them over its API.

tabctx: ask any regression predict for quantiles, such as a 90% interval per row, from the same model call as the mean, for every model it serves (prediction intervals).

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text: Model weights carry their own licenses. tabctx is Apache 2.0 and serves two models whose weights are licensed for commercial use, TabICLv2 (BSD-3) and TabDPT (Apache-2.0), next to TabPFN-3.5, whose weights are non-commercial unless licensed from Prior Labs. See the models table.

docs.title: When not to use tabctx
docs.text:
• One notebook, one table, one person: the model's own package is simpler.
  • Fit once, predict once: a server adds an upload and an HTTP round trip, with no fitted table to reuse.
  • You don't want to run a service: tabctx is a process to deploy and keep up. For several tables in one Python program, its engine runs in your own process.
  • No GPU and large tables: these models are slow on a CPU, with or without a server.
  • You want someone else to run the GPUs, and your data may leave your machines: a hosted API does that.

Try it: the quickstart runs a server on a laptop CPU and fits a real dataset.

docs.text: Issues and pull requests are welcome. Good places to start are issues labelled good first issue and help wanted, and adding a model.

docs.text:

docs.title: Pull requests

docs.title: Add a model
docs.text:
tabctx serves any tabular model that can split its work into encode a training table and predict against the encoding. A model is one class, a backend, plus a few lines of wiring. The cache, admission control, placement, tenancy and HTTP API come with it: none of them import a model, they only use this interface.

backends/tabdpt.py is a recent, compact example. Open requests for new models: Mitra (#102).

docs.title: The interface
docs.text:
class TabularICLBackend(Protocol):
    """A tabular in-context-learning model, wrapped for tabctx.

    Implementations MUST construct a fresh underlying estimator/model
    instance inside every fit() call. fit() mutates instance state (that's
    the whole point -- it's where the training context gets encoded), so
    reusing one shared instance across dataset_ids would silently corrupt
    every cached context that isn't the most recent one.
    """

    name: str

    def fit(self, X: ArrayLike, y: ArrayLike, task: Task) -> Any:
        """Encode the training context. Returns an opaque, backend-owned
        payload that the cache manager retains standalone (the engine never
        inspects it) and later passes back into predict()."""
        ...

    def predict(
        self,
        payload: Any,
        X_test: ArrayLike,
        return_proba: bool = False,
        quantiles: tuple[float, ...] | None = None,
    ) -> PredictOutcome:
        """Run inference against a cached context. Must be a SINGLE
        inference pass regardless of return_proba -- derive predictions from
        probabilities (e.g. argmax) rather than calling predict() and
        predict_proba() separately, since each call is a full forward pass
        over the cached context. A classification's labels are strings,
        whatever return_proba is (backends._outcome).

        quantiles: for a regression context only (the engine checks), the
        levels in (0, 1) at which to also return each row's predicted
        distribution, as PredictOutcome.quantiles -- from the same pass as
        the mean. A model that predicts only a point raises
        InvalidInputError."""
        ...

    def context_bytes_hint(self, n_train: int, n_features: int) -> int | None:
        """RESIDENT cost of the context most recently returned by fit(),
        for cache capacity/eviction accounting -- called by the engine
        AFTER fit(), not before, so an implementation can report a real
        measurement (e.g. actual device memory delta) instead of a guess.
        Return None if the backend has no opinion; the engine falls back
        to its own (much more conservative, pre-fit-only) MemoryEstimator.

        Implementations MAY also expose ``fit_peak_bytes_hint() -> int |
        None`` (optional; the engine probes with getattr): the TRANSIENT
        high-water memory of the most recent fit(). That is the
        admission-relevant quantity -- peak is what actually OOMs, and it
        can exceed the resident context by orders of magnitude -- and the
        engine feeds it (not the resident size) back into the estimator's
        admission learning."""
        ...

docs.title: What fit and predict receive
docs.text:
• X: a 2-D float32 numpy array. Missing values are NaN. Text columns arrive already encoded as category codes (0, 1, 2, ... in sorted order); a category the training table never had becomes NaN at predict. The model can treat every column as numeric.
  • y: the labels. For classification, any values (tabctx returns them as strings); for regression, numbers.
  • task: "classification" or "regression".

docs.title: The rules that matter
docs.text:
• A fresh model per fit. fit() must build a new underlying estimator every call; the payload it returns is cached and must not be shared with any other context.
  • One pass per predict. Derive labels from probabilities rather than running the model twice for return_proba=True (tabctx.backends._outcome.classification_outcome does it, and returns labels as strings).
  • Report the context's size. context_bytes_hint() returns the bytes the fitted context occupies, measured after the fit (on a GPU, the allocator's growth), or None to let the engine estimate it.
  • Raise tabctx's errors. Bad input raises InvalidInputError (HTTP 422); a device failure or out-of-memory raises BackendComputeError (507). Anything else reaches the caller as a
  • backends/tabpfn.py shows both.
  • name is the model id clients send as model and see in GET /v1/models, e.g. tabicl-v2.

docs.title: Optional hooks
docs.text:
The engine and the server probe for these with getattr, so a first version needs none of them:

Hook What it buys warmup() Load weights at server start, not inside the first tenant's fit. fit_peak_bytes_hint() The fit's real peak memory, which the admission estimator learns from. dumps_payload() / loads_payload() Compact spill files, e.g. leaving shared weights out. Default: pickle. prepare_fit() / fit_prepared() Run CPU preprocessing while another fit holds the GPU. may_offload() / host_bytes_estimate() Host-memory admission for fits that stage data in RAM.

docs.title: Wire it in
docs.text:
1. The backend, in src/tabctx/backends/<model>.py. Import the model's package inside the module (not in tabctx/__init__.py), so tabctx installs without it.
  2. The server: in src/tabctx/serve/factory.py, add its kind to BackendKind and BACKEND_KINDS, and a branch for it in _build_real_backend.
  3. The client: add its id to KNOWN_MODELS in src/tabctx/client.py, so the client finds it among a gateway's models.
  4. Packaging: an extra in pyproject.toml (tabctx[<model>]), added to the Dockerfile's export and to the image check in .github/workflows/docker_image.yml, and a row in the README's models table with the weights license.

docs.title: Memory calibration
docs.text:
Admission refuses a fit before it runs out of memory, using an estimate of the fit's peak memory by table shape. A new model starts with the fallback estimate (TabICL's, calibrated on an A100), which is conservative, and then learns from every fit's measured peak.

A calibrated model gets its own grid of measured peaks: benchmarks/calibrate_memory.py shows how they are measured (it drives TabICL today; point it at your backend), the grids live in src/tabctx/memory/, and factory.py maps each model to them (_REQUIREMENT_CALIBRATIONS, _PREDICT_CALIBRATIONS, _preloaded_observations). This can come in a later pull request.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Unit tests need no model weights: test your backend's own logic with small fakes, and use tabctx.backends.fake.FakeBackend for anything engine-side.
  • An integration test that skips without the package (pytest.importorskip) and checks that predictions through the backend match the model's own package on a small table (tests/integration/test_tabicl_kv_real.py is an example).
  • Accuracy: run benchmarks/eval_real_datasets.py against the model's own package and include the numbers in the pull request.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
The routes, with curl for the ones you'll use most. The reference has the full request and response schemas, generated from the service itself.

Method Route What it does POST /v1/tabctx/fit Encode a training table into a context. POST /v1/tabctx/predict Predict against a context. GET /v1/tabctx/datasets List your contexts. DELETE /v1/tabctx/datasets/{dataset_id} Delete a context everywhere it is held. POST /v1/tabctx/upload Stream a large table ahead of a fit or predict. GET /v1/models The models served; the default is marked. GET /v1/tabctx/limits What table shapes the deployment will admit right now. GET /v1/tabctx/residency Where your contexts are, per GPU (multi-GPU replicas). GET /livez, /readyz Liveness and readiness probes.

docs.title: Fit and predict
docs.text:
A table goes as rows of JSON, or as a file in the same request (CSV, gzip or zstd CSV, or Parquet).

Table fileJSON rows 
curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/fit \
  -F dataset_id=churn -F target=churned -F file=@train.parquet
curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/predict \
  -F dataset_id=churn -F return_proba=true -F file=@today.csv

curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/fit -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "dataset_id": "churn", "model": "tabicl-v2",
  "train_X": [[1.5, "gold", null], [0.2, "basic", 3.0]],
  "train_y": ["yes", "no"]}'
curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/predict -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "dataset_id": "churn", "test_X": [[1.1, "gold", 2.0]], "return_proba": true}'

Text cells are categories, null is a missing value, and the task is inferred from the labels unless you send task. A regression predict can also ask for quantiles of the predicted distribution, e.g. "quantiles": [0.05, 0.95] (-F quantiles=0.05,0.95 in a form), and gets quantiles (one row per test row) and quantile_levels back. When the training table was a file, a test file's columns are matched by name.

docs.title: Large tables
docs.text:
A table file sent with the fit or predict is fine up to TABCTX_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (4 GiB by default). To send it ahead, stream the CSV as the request body to /v1/tabctx/upload, then use the returned id once:

curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/upload -H 'x-session-id: churn' --data-binary @train.csv
# {"upload_id": "3f2a...", ...}
curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/fit -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"dataset_id": "churn", "train_upload_id": "3f2a...", "target": "churned"}'

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
A fit can carry ttl_s: the server deletes the context that many seconds later, from every tier (capped by the server's TABCTX_MAX_CONTEXT_AGE_S, which also applies to fits that don't ask). The fit response and the listing show expires_at.

curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/fit -F dataset_id=churn -F target=churned -F ttl_s=86400 -F file=@train.csv

docs.title: List and delete
docs.text:
curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/datasets
curl -X DELETE localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/datasets/churn

docs.title: Headers
docs.text: Header When x-tabctx-tenant-id Scopes every dataset id to a tenant. Required when the server runs with TABCTX_REQUIRE_TENANT=true. The server trusts it as sent: put it behind a gateway that sets it (see tenant isolation). x-session-id Equal to the dataset id. Routes the request to the replica holding the context when there are several. Authorization: Bearer ... Through a gateway that needs an API key.

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text: 422 malformed request · 404 no such context or upload · 413 too large to admit, or over the upload limit · 503 busy or temporarily unable, retry · 507 the model failed on the device · 401 tenant required.

docs.title: Estimators
docs.text:
TabctxClassifier and TabctxRegressor are scikit-learn estimators whose fitting and predicting happen on a tabctx server.

from tabctx import TabctxClassifier, TabctxRegressor, TabctxClient

client = TabctxClient("http://127.0.0.1:8000")
clf = TabctxClassifier(client=client)                       # the server's default model
reg = TabctxRegressor(model="tabpfn-3.5", client=client)    # or name one
  • Input: DataFrames or arrays. Text columns, categories, dates and missing values are sent as they are, as Parquet.
  • Labels may be strings, ints or bools; predict returns them as given to fit, and predict_proba's columns follow classes_.
  • scikit-learn tools: they clone and pickle, and work with cross_val_score and GridSearchCV.
  • One context per table: the context id is a hash of the table, model and task, so estimators fit on the same data share one cached context on the server.
  • Evicted or restarted servers are handled: an estimator keeps its training table and fits again if the server has lost the context.
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

cross_val_score(TabctxClassifier(client=client), X, y, cv=5)

docs.title: Prediction intervals
docs.text:
TabICL and TabPFN predict a distribution over the target, not just a number. predict_quantiles returns that distribution's quantiles, from the same model call as the mean:

reg = TabctxRegressor(client=client).fit(X_train, y_train)
q = reg.predict_quantiles(X_test, quantiles=[0.05, 0.5, 0.95])
low, median, high = q[:, 0], q[:, 1], q[:, 2]      # a 90% interval per row

Levels are in (0, 1), in any order; the columns follow it. Check the intervals on held-out data before relying on them: examples/prediction_intervals.py does it for California housing, where the 90% interval held 86.5% of the prices. Classifiers already return a distribution: predict_proba.

docs.title: The client
docs.text:
TabctxClient is the HTTP client underneath, pure standard library. It sets the routing and tenant headers for you.

client = TabctxClient("http://localhost:8000", tenant_id="acme")

client.fit(X_train, y_train, dataset_id="churn-v1")            # DataFrame, array or rows
client.fit_file("train.parquet", target="churned", dataset_id="churn-v2")
result = client.predict("churn-v1", X_test, return_proba=True)
result.predictions, result.probabilities, result.classes
client.predict("prices", X_test, quantiles=[0.05, 0.95]).quantiles  # regression

client.datasets()             # what the server holds for this tenant
client.delete("churn-v1")     # gone from GPU, host memory and disk
client.models(), client.limits()

base_url and api_key default to TABCTX_BASE_URL and TABCTX_API_KEY. The key is sent as a bearer token, never appears in the client's repr, and is left out when the client is pickled.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Server errors come back as tabctx exceptions, importable from tabctx. The in-process engine raises the same types for the same mistakes (invalid input, an unknown context, a table too large); conditions that are only temporary come back from a server as one retryable type, TabctxBackpressureError.

HTTP Exception Meaning 422 InvalidInputError A malformed request: retry won't help. 404 DatasetNotFoundError No such context: never fit, deleted, evicted, past its retention limit, or lost to a restart. Fit again. 404 UploadNotFoundError No such upload: expired, already used, or sent to another replica. 413 AdmissionRejected The table is too large for this deployment's memory, or the request for its upload limit. 503 TabctxBackpressureError Busy or temporarily unable; the client already retried with backoff. 507 BackendComputeError The model failed on the device. 401/403 PermissionError Missing tenant or API key.

docs.title: The engine in your own process
docs.text:
Without a server, TabctxEngine gives you the same cache and admission control in one Python process. This example uses the fake model, so it runs anywhere; swap in tabctx.backends.tabicl.TabICLBackend(device="cuda") (with the tabicl extra) for real predictions:

from tabctx import ContextCacheManager, TabctxEngine
from tabctx.backends.fake import FakeBackend
from tabctx.memory import A100_40GB_TABICL_CALIBRATION, PowerLawMemoryEstimator


def main() -> None:
    estimator = PowerLawMemoryEstimator(A100_40GB_TABICL_CALIBRATION)
    print(estimator.confidence())

    cache = ContextCacheManager(capacity_bytes=estimator.ceiling_bytes())
    engine = TabctxEngine(backend=FakeBackend(), cache=cache, estimator=estimator)

    X_train = [[float(i), float(i) * 2] for i in range(20)]
    y_train = ["a" if i % 2 == 0 else "b" for i in range(20)]
    dataset_id = engine.fit(
        X_train, y_train
    )  # task inferred: text labels -> classification
    print(f"fit -> dataset_id={dataset_id}")

    result = engine.predict(dataset_id, [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], return_proba=True)
    print(f"predict #1: {result.predictions} (proba shape reused cache)")

    # Reuse the same cached context for a different test batch -- no re-fit.
    result2 = engine.predict(dataset_id, [[5.0, 10.0]])
    print(f"predict #2 (cache reused): {result2.predictions}")

    print(f"stats: {engine.stats()}")
    engine.evict(dataset_id)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Run a tabctx server on your laptop, fit a real dataset and predict against it. A CPU is enough; the server uses a GPU if it finds one. tabctx needs Python 3.12 or newer.

docs.title: 1. Install and start a server
docs.text:
pip install "tabctx[standalone,tabicl,client]"
TABCTX_BACKEND=tabicl python -m tabctx.serve        # http://127.0.0.1:8000

The first start downloads the TabICLv2 weights (BSD-3, no account needed). curl localhost:8000/v1/models lists what the server serves.

docs.title: 2. Fit once, predict many
docs.text:
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_openml
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from tabctx import TabctxClassifier, TabctxClient

X, y = fetch_openml("credit-g", version=1, as_frame=True, return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)

clf = TabctxClassifier(client=TabctxClient("http://127.0.0.1:8000"))
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)          # encodes the table once, on the server
clf.score(X_test, y_test)          # 0.77, no training loop, no tuning
clf.predict_proba(X_test[:5])      # reuses the cached context

fit sends the table to the server, which encodes it into a cached context. Every later predict and predict_proba runs against that context, without encoding the table again. The DataFrame's text columns, categories and missing values go as they are.

docs.title: 3. On a GPU server
docs.text:
The container image includes TabICL, TabPFN and TabDPT; each model's weights download when the server starts.

docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 -e TABCTX_BACKEND=tabicl ghcr.io/vectorinstitute/tabctx

TABCTX_BACKEND=tabicl,tabdpt serves two models from one cache; a fit picks one with model=. Both are licensed for commercial use. tabpfn is a third choice, but its weights need you to accept Prior Labs' terms first (set TABPFN_TOKEN) and are licensed for non-commercial use.

docs.title: 4. Without Python
docs.text:
Every client is a thin wrapper over two calls:

curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/fit -F dataset_id=churn -F target=churned -F file=@train.csv
curl localhost:8000/v1/tabctx/predict -F dataset_id=churn -F file=@today.csv

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A server reads its settings from environment variables once, at start. Flags take 1/true or 0/false.

docs.title: Models and devices
docs.text: Variable Default TABCTX_BACKEND tabicl Comma-separated models to serve: tabicl, tabpfn, tabdpt, fake (no GPU or weights; for tests). The first is the default model. tabicl,tabdpt serves both from one cache. TABCTX_DEVICES auto auto: every visible GPU, else the CPU. Or a list such as cuda:0,cuda:1. Two or more devices place each table on one GPU. TABCTX_WORKER_PROCESSES 1 With several GPUs, one worker process per GPU (0: threads of one process). TABCTX_GPU_MEMORY_FRACTION 1.0 The share of each GPU this server may use, in (0, 1]. Lower it when replicas share a GPU. TABPFN_TOKEN Needed to download TabPFN weights, after accepting Prior Labs' terms.

docs.title: Cache and memory
docs.text: Variable Default TABCTX_SPILL_DIR off A directory for the disk tier: evicted contexts are written here and restored on their next predict. Measure on your disk first; a re-fit can be faster than a restore from a slow one. TABCTX_SPILL_CAPACITY_BYTES 50 GiB The disk tier's size, shared across GPUs. TABCTX_KV_CACHE kv TabICL's context: kv (fastest predicts), repr (much less memory per context), off (re-encode on every predict). TABCTX_KV_PRECISION int8 TabICL's cached keys and values: int8 (about half the memory; identical labels and metrics on 7 datasets, probabilities within 0.01), fp16, native. TABCTX_OFFLOAD_DIR <spill dir>/offload Where TabICL may stage a very large fit's intermediate results on disk.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: Variable Default TABCTX_MAX_CONTEXT_AGE_S no limit No fitted table is kept longer than this after its fit: it is deleted from device memory, host memory and the disk tier, within 30 s. It applies to every table, including those fit before it was set (a table spilled by tabctx < 0.19 has no recorded fit time and counts as expired). A fit can ask for less with ttl_s; GET /v1/tabctx/limits reports it.

docs.title: TabDPT
docs.text:
Variable Default TABCTX_TABDPT_CONTEXT_SIZE 2048 Training rows sampled as each predict's context. TabDPT keeps no encoding of the table, so a predict's cost grows with this, not with the table. TABCTX_TABDPT_ENSEMBLES 4 Ensemble members per predict.

The TABCTX_KV_* and TABCTX_COMPILE* settings apply to TabICL only.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text: Variable Default TABCTX_BATCH_WINDOW_MS 5 Concurrent predicts on one context within this window share one model call. 0 turns it off. TABCTX_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES 4 GiB The largest table file a request may carry. TABCTX_UPLOAD_TTL_S 3600 How long an unused /v1/tabctx/upload is kept.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Variable Default TABCTX_COMPILE 1 torch.compile TabICL's attention blocks at start (slower start, faster calls). TABCTX_COMPILE_AFTER_WARMUP 0 Also compile shapes first seen in requests, inside those requests. TABCTX_FAST_PREPROCESSING 1 Fit TabICL's Yeo-Johnson preprocessing on the GPU.

docs.title: Tenancy and routing
docs.text:
Variable Default TABCTX_REQUIRE_TENANT false true, 1 or yes: every request that reads or changes contexts must carry x-tabctx-tenant-id (else 401). /v1/tabctx/limits, /v1/models and the probes don't need it. RAY_SERVE_SESSION_ID_HEADER_KEY x-session-id The replica-affinity header, shared with Ray Serve's router.

The tenant header is trusted as sent

tabctx does not authenticate callers: any caller can send any tenant id. Tenancy is a security boundary only behind a gateway that authenticates each caller, sets x-tabctx-tenant-id itself and strips any value the client sent. See tenant isolation.

docs.title: Standalone host
docs.text:
python -m tabctx.serve [--host 0.0.0.0] [--port 8000]

Variable Default TABCTX_MAX_ONGOING_REQUESTS 8 Requests served at once. TABCTX_MAX_QUEUED_REQUESTS 16 Requests waiting for a slot; beyond that, 503. Health probes are never shed.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text: Variable TABCTX_BASE_URL Where TabctxClient() and the estimators send requests. TABCTX_API_KEY Sent as Authorization: Bearer (a gateway's key). TABCTX_MCP_HOME Where tabctx-mcp keeps fitted models (default .tabctx-mcp/). TABCTX_MCP_KEY_FILE The key tabctx-mcp signs saved models with (default ~/.config/tabctx-mcp/signing.key).

docs.title: TabctxEngine
docs.text:
TabctxEngine(backend: TabularICLBackend | None = None, cache: ContextCacheManager | None = None, estimator: MemoryEstimator | None = None, backends: dict[str, TabularICLBackend] | None = None, estimators: dict[str, MemoryEstimator] | None = None, default_backend: str | None = None, host_guard: HostMemoryGuard | None = None, device_baseline_bytes: int = 0, device_available: Callable[[], int | None] | None = None, expiry_sweep_s: float | None = None)

Orchestrates one or more backends over a single shared context cache and GPU budget. Multi-backend serving (e.g. TabICL and TabPFN behind one endpoint) works because every cached context remembers which backend fit it (CachedContext.backend_name): fit() picks a backend, predict() dispatches to whichever one owns the context. Memory estimates are per-backend (models peak differently for the same shape) while admission headroom is global (they share the device).

Single-backend form: TabctxEngine(backend=, cache=, estimator=). Multi-backend form: TabctxEngine(backends={name: b}, cache=, estimators={name: e}, default_backend=name).

docs.title: fit
docs.text:
fit(X: ArrayLike, y: ArrayLike, task: Task | None = None, dataset_id: str | None = None, backend: str | None = None, schema: TableSchema | None = None, expires_at: float | None = None) -> str

Encode and cache a training context. Returns a dataset_id to pass to predict() -- generated automatically unless the caller supplies one (e.g. to reuse a stable, caller-known identifier).

expires_at (unix time): when the context is deleted, from every tier, whatever else happens (a retention limit); None keeps it until evicted or deleted.

schema (optional) records how the training table's columns were encoded (tabctx.schema) on the cached context, for callers that encode test tables the same way; the engine itself only ever checks feature count.

Raises InvalidInputError for malformed input (mismatched X/y lengths, empty tables, ragged rows) before anything else -- checked first so a careless client's bad request can't reach the backend as an unhandled exception.

Raises AdmissionRejected before any backend/GPU work if the training shape alone is estimated to exceed the configured memory ceiling (using the conservative formula-based estimator -- this pre-fit gate must stay conservative since nothing has run yet to measure).

The context's cache-accounting size (used for capacity/eviction bookkeeping, not for this admission gate) is queried from the backend AFTER fit() completes, not before: a real backend can measure actual post-fit GPU memory now that the fit has happened, which is far more accurate than any pre-fit estimate. Confirmed empirically this mattered -- the formula-based estimate ran ~14x higher than real measured GPU memory for a realistic multi-tenant shape, needlessly throttling how many contexts actually fit.

docs.title: predict
docs.text:
predict(dataset_id: str, X_test: ArrayLike, return_proba: bool = False, quantiles: Sequence[float] | None = None) -> PredictOutcome

Predict against a previously-fit context, reusing its cached training-context encoding. quantiles (regression only): also return each row's predicted distribution at these levels in (0, 1) (tabctx.uncertainty); InvalidInputError for a classification context. Large test sets are automatically chunked (see chunking.py) against the memory ceiling -- this is the one thing that must never let a single request take down the replica, which the naive one-shot wrapper this library replaces did not do.

A light predict (a resident context, at most LIGHT_PREDICT_ROWS test rows) runs beside a fit on this device; larger ones wait for the device's fits, and a spilled context is restored first.

Convenience matching the one-shot semantics of the wrapper this library replaces: fit, predict once, evict. Prefer fit()+predict() directly when the same training set will be queried more than once -- that's the entire point of tabctx's caching.

docs.title: ContextCacheManager
docs.text:
ContextCacheManager(capacity_bytes: int, policy: EvictionPolicy | None = None, spill_store: Any | None = None, max_age_s: float | None = None)

spill_store: optional disk tier (cache/spill.py). When set, capacity-pressure evictions spill instead of dropping, and get() transparently reloads spilled contexts. Explicit evict() (caller intent, re-fit overwrite) never spills -- and also drops any spilled copy, so an evicted context can't resurrect.

docs.title: put
docs.text:
put(context: CachedContext) -> list[str]

Insert a context, evicting via the policy to make room first. Returns the list of evicted dataset_ids. Raises CacheCapacityError if context.est_bytes alone exceeds total capacity -- no amount of eviction would ever make room for it. Overwriting an existing dataset_id replaces it in both tiers (a stale spilled copy must never outlive the context that superseded it); the id stays visible to has() throughout.

docs.title: get
docs.text:
get(dataset_id: str) -> CachedContext | None

The resident context, else a spilled one reloaded and re-admitted (its displacements may spill in turn). The reload runs outside the lock; callers serialize restores of one device (the engine does so under its fit lock).

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete(dataset_id: str, settle_timeout_s: float = 600.0) -> tuple[CachedContext | None, bool]

Drop a context from every tier. Returns the resident one (the caller decides when its memory may be released) and whether there was a copy in any tier. Never spills: this is caller intent (an explicit delete, fit_predict's one-shot cleanup), and a spilled copy left behind would silently resurrect on the next get().

Atomic with respect to moves between tiers: it first waits for a spill, restore or replacement of this id to land (else a spill write finishing afterwards would bring the context back), then removes both copies under the lock, so no get() or evict_one() can see one copy gone and the other still there. The spilled copy goes first: if unlinking it fails, the resident copy is untouched. Its two unlinks are short, though a multi-GB file can take ~0.1 s, and bookkeeping (light predicts' peek and touch) waits meanwhile. Raises CacheUnavailableError if the move doesn't land in settle_timeout_s (nothing is deleted then: retry).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
tabctx error types.

Kept HTTP-agnostic on purpose -- a serving layer (e.g. serve/app.py) maps these to status codes at its own boundary, so the engine stays usable outside of any particular transport.

docs.title: TabctxError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

Base class for all tabctx errors.

docs.title: InvalidInputError
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Raised for malformed input (mismatched X/y lengths, empty tables, ragged rows, a predict() feature count that doesn't match the cached context) -- checked before any backend/GPU work is attempted. Found via load testing: without this, malformed input reached the backend and raised an unhandled, untranslated exception (numpy/sklearn shape errors), surfacing as a raw 500 that leaked no useful detail to the caller -- exactly the failure mode a multi-tenant service can't afford (one careless client's bad request shouldn't look like a server bug).

docs.title: AdmissionRejected
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Raised when a request's estimated memory footprint exceeds the configured ceiling, before any backend/GPU work is attempted.

docs.title: DatasetNotFoundError
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Raised when predict() is called with a dataset_id that isn't cached (never fit, evicted, or lost to a replica restart).

docs.title: CacheCapacityError
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Raised when a single context's estimated size alone exceeds the cache's total capacity -- no amount of eviction would make room.

docs.title: UploadNotFoundError
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Raised when fit()/predict() references an upload_id that isn't present on this replica (never uploaded, expired, already consumed, or -- in a multi-replica deployment -- uploaded without the session affinity header, so it landed on a different replica).

docs.title: UploadTooLargeError
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Raised when a streamed upload exceeds the configured size cap, before the excess is written to disk.

docs.title: BackendComputeError
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Wraps a backend-level compute failure (e.g. a CUDA OOM that slipped past admission control) so callers don't need to import torch to catch tabctx errors.

docs.title: CacheUnavailableError
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Raised when contexts can't be listed or deleted correctly right now: a GPU worker is dead (its spilled copies would outlive a delete) or didn't answer, or a context is still moving between cache tiers. Nothing is deleted where it couldn't be done; retryable, so the API answers 503.

docs.title: HostMemoryUnavailableError
docs.text:
Bases: TabctxError

Raised when host-memory admission can't be decided right now (its shared accounting is stuck, e.g. a worker died holding the lock); retryable, so the API answers 503.
